message.content:
Lion (Panthera leo) is a member of the order **Carnivora** (family Felidae), while zebra (Equus quagga) belongs to the order **Perissodactyla** (family Equidae).  
Their most recent common ancestor is therefore a small, probably insect‑eating mammal that lived roughly **70–80 million years ago** and belonged to the clade **Laurasiatheria**—the group that gave rise to many modern land mammals such as ungulates, carnivores, bats, and whales.  

In other words, the last common ancestor of lion and zebra was a small, early Laurasiatherian mammal that existed long before the diversification of the specific lineages that led to cats and horses.

But they share a more distant common ancestor at the level of class Mammalia. But maybe they want the most recent common ancestor (MRCA). Lion is a cat, zebra is an equid. The MRCA would be a mammalian ancestor that gave rise to both the lineage leading to cats (Felidae) and the lineage leading to horses (Equidae). That ancestor would be a member of the clade Euarchontoglires? Wait, felids are part of the order Carnivora, which is part of the clade Laurasiatheria. Equids are part of Perissodactyla, also part of Laurasiatheria. So the MRCA of lion and zebra would be a member of the clade Laurasiatheria, likely a small mammal that lived around 70 million years ago. Or "the last common ancestor of all placental mammals." But the lion and zebra diverged earlier than that. Actually, the last common ancestor of Carnivora and Perissodactyla is the ancestor of the clade Laurasiatheria. That ancestor existed about 70-80 million years ago. So the answer: "The last common ancestor of lion and zebra is a small, probably insectivorous mammal that lived around 70-80 million years ago, belonging to the clade Laurasiatheria."
